newsitem.title: PERU: Rebels fire shots in Peru siege's war of nerves.
newsitem.headline: Rebels fire shots in Peru siege's war of nerves.

text.p: Marxist rebels holding 73 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima fired several warning shots into the air on Wednesday as police stepped up a tense war of nerves at the besieged house, witnesses said.

Following unusual movements by their special forces units in front of the compound on Tuesday, police sent a helicopter flying overhead and moved in black armoured personnel carriers with heavy machineguns to within two blocks.

There was no immediate response by the rebels, although during the night they unfurled a new banner on the roof of the residence pledging not to give up. "Surrender is not the path for Tupac Amaru followers," it read.

About 15 heavily-armed members of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA), who take their name from an 18th-century Indian leader who led an uprising against Spanish colonial rule, stormed the house during a diplomatic reception Dec. 17 in honour of Japanese Emperor Akihito.
The white police helicopter flew over the compound four or five times, maintaining height and not buzzing the rebels. Local radio station Radio Programas said top police chiefs were aboard the craft.
Two black, Russian-made Caspir armoured personnel carriers then drove around the residence and parked near by, one aiming its heavy machinegun towards the compound.

Otherwise, daily routines established during the 36-day siege continued, with International Committee of the Red Cross representative Michel Minnig and Roman Catholic Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani visiting the hostages and rebels. Neither spoke to reporters upon leaving.
Soldiers sprinkled water on their heads as temperatures in Lima rose into the 80s Fahrenheit (above 26 degrees Celsius).
Police earlier said the rebel shots in the night were to tell them to stay back.
"They're warning us not to get too close," a police officer about a block from the residence told Reuters.

In a clear signal to the rebels that Tokyo and Lima were united on how to handle the crisis, Japan's Lower House of parliament passed a resolution denouncing them for "conducting criminal acts against the international community."

"We confirm the basic principle of not giving in to terrorism and urge the government to work toward a peaceful resolution of the crisis with the top priority on the lives of the hostages," the resolution approved unanimously by the 500- seat Lower House said.

President Alberto Fujimori, who says the main rebel demand of freedom for some 400 of their jailed colleagues is unacceptable, also basked in the approval of Washington for his handling of the crisis.

Fujimori "has been admirable in the way he's handled this problem," U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters on Tuesday, in remarks trumpeted by Lima's pro-government press on Wednesday.
The rebels, who have booby-trapped and mined the compound against possible attack, have fired warning shots on several occasions since the siege began. No one has been injured.
The police movements and shots came as talks to end the crisis remained on hold.

Red Cross officials have scouted out several possible locations near the residence for proposed talks between MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa and government negotiator Domingo Palermo, Fujimori's education minister.
The rebels say they are ready to talk but that there is no point if their main demand for the release of their comrades is not on the agenda.
The MRTA initially took about 500 hostages after storming the residence but have released most in what they called "goodwill gestures."

The remaining 73 include two Peruvian ministers, generals, security chiefs, about two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats and the Japanese and Bolivian ambassadors as well as Fujimori's younger brother Pedro.
